stages.name: Comparative advantage and trade patterns
stages.title: Comparative advantage and trade patterns
stages.sub: Why countries end up trading the particular goods they do, with the particular partners they do.

steps.q: You worked out that Vietnam gives up less to produce a tonne of rice than the UK does, while the UK gives up less to produce a tonne of cars. If both countries want to gain from trade, what should Vietnam do with its production?
steps.hint: Which good does Vietnam sacrifice least to make?

steps.q: Vietnam now produces far more rice than it needs at home. What does it do with the surplus?
steps.wrong: Store it for future domestic use only
steps.hint: If a country makes more of something than it consumes, where does the rest go?

steps.q: Vietnam has stopped producing many cars because the UK produces them at lower opportunity cost. Where do Vietnam's cars now come from?
steps.hint: If Vietnam no longer specialises in cars, but still wants them, what must happen?

steps.q: Suppose Thailand also has a low opportunity cost in rice, similar to Vietnam's. Would the UK gain much by buying its cars-for-rice trade specifically with Thailand rather than Vietnam?
steps.right: No, either country would do fine
steps.wrong: Yes, only Vietnam would do fine
steps.hint: What matters is the opposite side's opportunity cost, not the country's name.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Countries tend to export the goods they produce at low opportunity cost, and import the goods other countries produce more cheaply in opportunity-cost terms. If every country does this, what does world trade look like?
steps.right: Each country's exports are its cheapest goods
steps.wrong: Each country exports and imports at random
steps.hint: Think about the big picture that all the specialising, exporting and importing adds up to.
